'''ʻAfīf al-Dīn ʻAlī ibn ʻAdlān al-Mawsilī''' ({{langx|ar|عفيف لدين علي بن عدلان الموصلي }}; 1187–1268 CE), born in [[Mosul]], was an [[Arab]] [[cryptologist]], linguist and poet who is known for his early contributions to [[cryptanalysis]], to which he dedicated at least two books. He was also involved in [[literature]] and [[poetry]], and taught on the Arabic language at the [[Salihiyya Madrasa|Al-Salihiyya Mosque]] of Cairo.

He was in contact with various rulers of his time, and in this capacity he gained practical experience in cryptanalysis or the science of breaking encoded messages. He dedicated ''On Cryptanalysis,'' his only surviving work on the topic'','' to [[Al-Ashraf Musa, Emir of Damascus|Al-Ashraf Musa]] ({{reign|1229|1237}}), the [[Ayyubid dynasty|Ayyubid]] Emir of Damascus. He wrote three other books, including  ''Al-Mu'lam'' (''The Told [Book]''), also on cryptanalysis, but it is now lost.  ''On Cryptanalysis'' is a sort of guidebook for cryptanalysts, containing twenty sets of techniques he calls "rules". The methods contains more practical details than [[Al-Kindi]]'s [[8th century]] ''Treatise on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages''—the earliest surviving work on cryptoanalysis—but lack its predecessor's theoretical background on cryptography. Among Ibn 'Adlan's original contributions were methods for breaking no-space [[Substitution cipher|monoalphabetic]] cryptograms, a type of ciphers which were developed to evade analysis techniques described earlier by Al-Kindi. In this treatise Ibn 'Adlan also includes a real-life example of a cryptogram that he deciphered and his full process in breaking it, which, in the words of the cryptographer [[James Massey]], provides "the authentic experience of a highly skilled cryptanalyst."

== Biography ==
[[File:Cairo, madrasa al-zazer 01.JPG|thumb|Ibn 'Adlan worked as a teacher at the [[Salihiyya Madrasa|Al-Salihiyya Mosque]] complex (remaining parts pictured in 2015).]]
'Afif al-Din 'Ali ibn 'Adlan was born in Mosul in 583 [[Hijri year|AH]] ({{circa|1187 CE}}).{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=13}} He was of an Arab origin{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=98}} and received education in Baghdad, including lessons on [[syntax]] by the grammarian [[Abu al-Baqa al-Ukbari]].{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=13}} Subsequently, he lived in Damascus for a time,{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=113}} before became a teacher of the Arabic language at the [[Salihiyya Madrasa|Al-Salihiyya Mosque]] of Cairo until his death in 666 AH (c. 1268 CE).{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=13}} In addition to writing treatises on linguistics and [[cryptanalysis]], he was considered an authority in literature and wrote poems himself.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=13}}{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=281}} He was in contact with various rulers, and in this capacity he gained practical experience in cryptanalysis, which he calls ''hall al-mutarjam''. One of these rulers was [[Al-Ashraf Musa, Emir of Damascus|Al-Ashraf Musa]] ({{reign|1229|1237}}), the [[Ayyubid dynasty|Ayyubid]] Emir of Damascus, for whom he dedicated his treatise ''On Cryptanalysis''.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=14}} He was also known by his multiple [[Nisba (onomastics)|''nisbas'']] (descriptive epithets): al-Mawsili (of Mosul), al-Nahwi (the Grammarian) and al-Mutarjim (the Cryptoanalyst).{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=113}}

==Works==
[[File:Ibn 'Adlan - On Cryptanalysis, Al-mu'allaf lil-malik al-'Ashraf, 13th century.jpg|thumb|The cover (''right'') and the first page (''left'') of Ibn Adlan's ''On Cryptanalysis'']]
Early Arabic bibliographies attributed three titles to him, including one on cryptanalysis, ''Fi hall al-mutarjam'' (''On Cryptanalysis''), also known as ''Al-mu'allaf lil-malik al-'Ashraf'' (''The [Book] Written for King al-Ashraf''). In addition, a reference in ''On Cryptanalysis'' points to another book, ''Al-Mu'lam'' (''The Told [Book]''), which is now lost, in which he describes algorithms for analysing cryptograms. His other two works were titled ''Al-Intihab li-kashf al-'abyat al-mushkilat al-i'rab'' and ''<nowiki>'Uqlat al-mujtaz fi hall al-aljaz</nowiki>''.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=13}}

=== Background ===
The practice and study of encrypting messages into ciphers, called [[History of cryptography|cryptography]], had existed since [[ancient history|ancient times]], practised by the Egyptian, Chinese, Indian, Mesopotamian, Greek, and Roman civilisations.{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=103}} In contrast, [[cryptanalysis]], the science of breaking ciphers—in other words, recovering the plain message from an encrypted one—was founded in the [[Spread of Islam|early Arab-Muslim civilisation]].{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|pp=103–104}}{{sfn|Broemeling|2011|p=255}} The earliest surviving work found on the topic of cryptanalysis is the ''Risalah fi Istikhraj al-Mu'amma'' ("Treatise on Deciphering Cryptographic Messages") written by [[Al-Kindi]] (c. 801–873), an Arab scholar who also wrote on other topics including philosophy, astronomy, and medicine.{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=106}}{{sfn|Broemeling|2011|p=255}}{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=280}} Reports are also found on other works before al-Kindi, among the earliest of which is ''al-Mu'amma'' ("The Book of Cryptographic Messages"), written by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad in the 8th century, but they are now lost.{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=98}}{{sfn|Broemeling|2011|p=255}} Al-Kindi's book presents cryptanalysis techniques such as [[frequency analysis]], which is to also be covered by Ibn 'Adlan's works.{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=106}}

=== ''On Cryptanalysis'' ===
[[File:Cour mosquee Suleymaniye Istanbul.jpg|thumb|''On Cryptanalysis'' is preserved in the library of the [[Süleymaniye Mosque]] of Istanbul (''mosque pictured in 2011'').]]
''On Cryptanalysis'' was written in a style of a handbook or a manual, describing Ibn 'Adlan's twenty "rules" or techniques of cryptanalysis, grouped into nine themes.{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=281}}{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=113}} Unlike the cryptological treatises of Al-Kindi before him and later [[Ibn al-Durayhim]] (c. 1312–1361), which provide theoretical background on cryptography including systematic explanations on types of ciphers, Ibn 'Adlan's ''On Cryptanalysis'' focuses on the practical matters and specific methods in breaking encrypted texts of his time, often in a more detailed manner than Al-Kindi.{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=281}} The work's introduction section does include a brief description of the [[simple substitution]] encipherment method, and encourages its readers to read other sources to learn about other methods.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|pp=16–17}}

One of Ibn 'Adlan's most original contribution in this treatise is the cryptanalysis of no-space [[Substitution cipher|monoalphabetic]] cryptograms (''al-mudmaj'')—encrypted texts that do not include [[Space (punctuation)|a space]] to denote separation between words.{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=281}}{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=24}} This type of cryptograms was not mentioned by al-Kindi: it was developed by subsequent cryptographers (code makers) in order to counteract the cryptographic attacks described in his works, part of a kind of [[arms race]] between the code makers and code breakers. In the west, this type of cryptanalysis was only attested in the sixteenth century in the works of the Italian [[Giambattista della Porta]]. According to ibn 'Adlan, the cryptographers of his time "allege that their ciphers can defy detection and analysis" by using the no-space method.{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=281}} Ibn 'Adlan recommended the use of frequency analysis,{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|pp=80}} as well as the analysis of consecutive letters based on knowing how many times each letter can possibly occur consecutively in Arabic sentences and the specific ways they can do so.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|pp=21–22}}  He also wrote on the analysis of ciphers in which the space is represented by variable symbols.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=19}}{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=281}}

''On Cryptanalysis'' also deals with frequency analysis: Ibn 'Adlan follows al-Kindi's data on the [[Arabic letter frequency|frequency of Arabic letters]]—although Al-Kindi does not receive any direct attribution, the numbers provided by the two authors are identical—{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=18}}and divided the Arabic alphabet into seven common (frequently-occurring), eleven medium, and ten rare letters.{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=113}} Ibn 'Adlan presents a table of the most common two or three letter words, and offers a minimum sample size, a lower limit of text length that can be cryptoanalysed using its frequency of letters: about 90 characters (approximately three times the length of the Arabic alphabet).{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=113}}{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|pp=18–19}} Below this limit, according to Ibn 'Adlan the occurrence of letters will not follow the provided frequency distribution.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=19}}

The treatise includes the cryptanalysis of common adjacent letters, the [[Arabic definite article]] ال (al-, 'the'), and letters frequently occurring at the beginning or the end of a word. Ibn 'Adlan also writes on the probable words in the opening and closing section of a text (such as the Arabic formula [[Basmala|Bismillah]], "In the name of God").{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|pp=19–20}} He adds special principles for analysing encrypted poetry, including the knowledge of prosody, rhymes and meters.{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=22}} He then explains his cryptanalysis steps, moving from the ciphertext to possible solutions, then to the suspected, the probable, and eventually the confirmed solution.{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|pp=113–115}} In the closing section of the book, Ibn 'Adlan includes a real-life example of a cryptogram that he broke and his full process in deciphering it, including his false starts, thought process, and eventual solution. The cryptographer [[James Massey]] describes this section as "intriguing" and providing "the authentic experience of a highly skilled cryptanalyst."{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=281}}

A copy of ''On Cryptanalysis'' is preserved in the library of the [[Süleymaniye Mosque]] of Istanbul (manuscript number 5359).{{sfn|Mrayati|Meer Alam|at-Tayyan|2004|p=13}} A modern edition was prepared by editors Muhammad Mrayati, Yahya Meer Alam and Hassan al-Tayyan and published by the [[Arab Academy of Damascus]] in 1987, including introductions and explanatory materials from the editors. It was translated into English in 2004.{{sfn|Massey|2008|p=280}}{{sfn|Al-Kadi|1992|p=113, also p. 125 no. 12}}
